We need to find minimum operations to obtain a subsequence whose sum equals target, starting from array of powers of 2, allowed operation: split any element >1 into two halves (each half = value/2). Each split counts as one operation.

Goal: produce a multiset (order doesn't matter for subsequence existence) of elements such that we can select a subset (subsequence) whose sum is exactly target. Since the order doesn't affect existence of a subsequence with given multiset (any subset can be selected as subsequence, as long as we maintain original order? Actually subsequence retains order relative to original array, but we can delete any elements; if we need a specific multiset, we can always pick them in the order they appear after splits? Since we can insert splits at the end (the operation adds two halves to the end). This means new elements are appended at end. So original order of existing elements stays same, and new elements go to end. Subsequence can pick elements in order they appear. Since we can always pick needed elements as they appear (they may be interspersed with other elements, but we can skip others). So any multiset of elements that we can generate via splits can be used as subsequence (we can ignore other elements). So order not restrictive.

Thus problem reduces to: Starting from multiset of given powers of two (nums), we can repeatedly split any element >1 into two equal halves. Each split increases total count of elements by 1 (replace one element with two). We want to achieve a multiset that contains a subset summing to target. Equivalent: we want to be able to form target as sum of some of the elements we have (each used at most as many times as present). Since all numbers are powers of two, this is like we have counts of each power of two, and we can split higher powers into lower ones (cost = number of splits needed). Want minimal total splits to make it possible to represent target using available counts (after splitting). Splitting a 2^k into two 2^{k-1} costs 1 operation, and increases count of 2^{k-1} by 2 while decreasing count of 2^{k} by 1. This is like we can break down higher bits into lower bits at cost.

Goal: achieve that for each bit position i (0-indexed), we have enough count of 2^i to cover the binary representation of target, using available counts
